summary.title: A Brief, Incomplete, and Mostly Wrong History of Programming Languages
summary.one_liner: A satirical, year-by-year timeline of programming languages from Jacquard's loom (1801) to Scala (2003), where the jokes are built on real language histories and their common criticisms.
takeaways: Gives a chronological overview of major languages from the 1800s through 2003, including who created each and roughly when.
Shows that many well-known languages share design lineage, such as Java and C# having nearly identical feature lists.
Explains briefly why some languages are described as functional, logic, object-oriented, or ML-family, through humorous but recognizable examples.
Is explicitly not a reliable source: the author flags many claims as jokes, and one note says a claim about Ruby's creation is false.
summary.summary: This is a humorous blog post listing programming languages in chronological order, from Jacquard's punch-card loom in 1801 to Scala in 2003. Each entry pairs a real language, its creator and date with fictional or exaggerated anecdotes and jabs at language features and communities. The post's title says it is mostly wrong, and it includes an editor's note that one claim about Ruby's origin is false. It is useful mainly as a light overview of which languages came from which people and periods, not as a factual reference.
